intro: A bean sprouts in a cup. A bee lands on a purple flower. A rabbit freezes in tall grass. What do these living things need? Where do they live? In this unit, you will find out.

You will learn to tell living from nonliving. You will see what plants and animals need. You will meet parents and their young. You will visit ponds, forests, prairies and deserts. You will see how living things change the land, and how people can care for it.
bigQuestion: What do living things need, and how does the place they live give it to them?

timeline.t: Mia puts a bean seed in a cup of dirt and waters it.
Nothing shows. Mia waters the dirt again and waits.
A crack opens in the dirt. A pale loop pushes up.
Two leaves open. They turn toward the window.
Leo's bean in the closet is yellow. Mia's is green.
Mia forgets to water. The leaves droop.
Mia waters the bean. The leaves stand up again.
The stem is tall. Mia ties it to a stick.
Small white flowers open. A bee visits.
Green pods hang down. Inside are new bean seeds.

words.d: alive; it grows, needs water and air, and makes more of its kind
not alive; it does not grow, eat or make babies
a safe place to rest and stay warm and dry
a line that shows who eats what
the place where a plant or animal lives and gets what it needs
land of tall grass and wildflowers, with few trees
an animal that carries pollen from flower to flower
to stay alive

test.why: A bee eats, grows and makes more bees. Clouds and pencils do not.

test.q: Leo's bean turned yellow in the closet. What did it need?
test.why: The bean had water and air. It was missing light.

test.q: Which need does a rabbit's hole meet?
test.why: The hole is a safe place. It keeps the rabbit warm and hidden.

test.q: A rabbit eats clover. A fox eats the rabbit. Where did the clover get its energy?
test.why: Plants make food using sunlight. That is where every food chain starts.

test.q: What does a squirrel do that changes the land?
choices: Buries acorns that grow into trees
test.why: Forgotten acorns sprout into oak trees. The squirrel plants a forest by accident.

choices: look alike, but not exactly the same
test.why: Young look like their parents. But size and color can be different.

test.q: Why does a parent bird bring worms to the nest?
choices: Baby birds cannot get food yet
The nest needs worms to stay together
test.why: Baby birds cannot fly or hunt. Their parents feed them.

test.q: A finch's short, thick beak is good for...
test.why: A short, thick beak works like a nutcracker on hard seeds.

test.q: Which animal fits a desert habitat?
choices: A frog on a lily pad
A lizard that hides under rocks
test.why: A desert is dry and hot. A lizard hides under rocks in the heat.

test.q: A bee carries pollen from flower to flower. What can the flower make now?
test.why: Pollen from another flower lets a flower make seeds.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is a bean plant living or nonliving? Use evidence from Mia's bean cup and from what plants need. Tell why your evidence proves your claim.
tips: Claim: say it in one sentence. 'A bean plant is living.'
Evidence: what did the bean do? It sprouted. It grew leaves. It drooped without water.
Reasoning: living things grow and need water, light and air. The bean did all of that.
The other side: someone might say a plant is not alive because it does not move. What would you tell them?

title: Living Things and Where They Live

chapters.title: What Plants and Animals Need
chapters.bigQuestion: What do plants and animals need to stay alive, and how do they change the places they live?

story.title: The Bean in the Cup
story.kicker: A tiny seed sat in a cup of dirt on the windowsill. What would it do?
paragraphs: Mia put a bean seed in a paper cup. She added dirt. She poured in a little water. She set the cup on the sunny windowsill. Then she waited. Day 1, nothing. Day 2, nothing. The dirt just sat there.

On Day 4, Mia saw a crack in the dirt. A pale loop was pushing up. It was the bean! It bent like a tiny green neck. By Day 6, two leaves opened. They turned toward the window. They were reaching for the light.

Mia's friend Leo did a test. He put his bean cup in a dark closet. He gave it water too. His bean came up. But it was thin and yellow. It leaned and flopped. It looked sick. Then Leo moved it to the window. In three days, it turned green.

Mia forgot to water her bean over the weekend. On Monday, the leaves drooped. She gave it water. By lunch, the leaves stood up again. The bean was alive. It needed things, just like Mia did. It needed water. It needed light. And it needed air.
story.think: Leo's bean turned yellow in the closet. What did it need? How do you know?

lessons.title: Living and Nonliving
lessons.mainIdea: Living things grow, need food and water, and make more of their kind.
reading: Look around your room. A cat is *living*. A rock is *nonliving*. How can you tell? Living things grow. They need water. They need air. They make new living things like themselves.
A rock does not grow. It does not eat or drink. It never has baby rocks. A toy car moves, but only when you push it. It does not need food. So it is nonliving.
A tree does not walk. But it is living. It grows taller each year. It drinks water with its roots. It makes seeds. Seeds grow into new trees.

words.d: alive; it grows, needs water and air, and makes more of its kind
not alive; it does not grow, eat or make babies

look.title: A Robot Dog and a Real Dog
look.text: A robot dog walks. It barks. It wags its tail. Then its battery runs out. It stops. A real dog eats. It drinks. It grows from a puppy. One day it can have puppies of its own.
look.prompt: Which dog is living? What clues tell you?

check.q: Which one is living?
check.why: A tree grows, drinks water with its roots, and makes seeds.

check.q: Why is a rock nonliving?
choices: It is too heavy to move
It does not grow or need food
check.why: Living things grow and need food and water. A rock does neither.

check.q: A toy car moves. Is it living?
choices: No. It only moves when you push it.
check.why: Moving is not enough. A toy car does not grow, eat or make new toy cars.

lessons.title: Signs of Life
lessons.mainIdea: You can find clues that show something is alive.
reading: Scientists look for clues. Does it grow? Does it need water? Does it need air? Does it make babies or seeds? If the answer is yes, it is living.
Some clues are tricky. A river moves. A fire grows bigger. But a river does not eat. A fire does not have baby fires that grow up. They are nonliving.
Mold on old bread is living. It grows. It spreads. It takes water from the bread. Even tiny things can be alive.

words.d: something you notice that helps you find an answer

look.title: The Puddle and the Plant
look.text: After rain, a puddle sits next to a small plant. The next day, the puddle is smaller. The plant is a little taller. A week later, the puddle is gone. The plant has a new leaf.
look.prompt: Which one is living, the puddle or the plant? What clues tell you?

check.q: Which clue shows that something is living?
check.why: Growing and needing water are signs of life. Wet things and moving things can be nonliving.

check.q: A fire grows bigger. Is fire living?
choices: No. It does not eat or make babies that grow.
check.why: Fire gets bigger, but it does not eat, drink or make baby fires. It is nonliving.

check.q: Mold on bread is...
choices: nonliving, because it does not walk
living, because it grows and spreads
check.why: Mold grows, spreads and takes water. Those are signs of life, even in tiny things.

lessons.title: Plants Need Water, Light and Air
lessons.mainIdea: A plant needs water, light and air to grow.
reading: A plant cannot walk to a store. It makes its own food. It uses *sunlight*. It uses air. It uses water. Take one away, and the plant gets sick.
*Roots* drink water from the dirt. Leaves catch light. Leaves also take in air. That is why leaves are flat and wide. They spread out to catch the sun.
Remember Leo's bean in the closet? It had water and air. It had no light. It turned yellow and weak. Light was the missing thing.

words.d: light from the sun; plants use it to make their food
the parts of a plant under the ground; they drink water

look.title: Two Cups on a Shelf
look.text: Ana has two bean plants. Both sit on the windowsill. She waters Cup A every day. She never waters Cup B. After one week, Cup A is tall and green. Cup B is brown and dry.
look.prompt: What did Cup B need? How did Ana's test show it?

check.q: What do roots do?
check.why: Roots are under the ground. They take in water for the plant.

check.q: A plant in a dark closet gets water. What will happen?
check.why: Plants need light to make food. Without light, Leo's bean turned yellow and floppy.

check.q: Why are leaves flat and wide?
choices: To hold water like a cup
To catch more light and air
check.why: Flat, wide leaves spread out. That lets them catch lots of sunlight and air.

lessons.title: Animals Need Food, Water, Air and Shelter
lessons.mainIdea: Animals need food, water, air and a safe place to live.
reading: A plant makes its own food. An animal cannot. A rabbit must find food. It eats clover. A robin pulls up worms. A fox hunts mice.
Animals need water too. A deer drinks from a creek. Animals need air. A fish takes air from the water with its *gills*. A whale swims up to breathe.
Animals also need *shelter*. Shelter is a safe place. A bird builds a nest. A rabbit digs a hole. Shelter keeps animals warm and dry. It hides them from danger.

words.d: a safe place to rest and stay warm and dry
parts of a fish that take air out of the water

look.title: Setting Up a Hamster Cage
look.text: You get a pet hamster. You hang a water bottle in the cage. You fill a dish with food. You add a little plastic house. The cage has holes in the top, so air gets in.
look.prompt: Name the four things the hamster needs. Which thing in the cage gives each one?

check.q: What is shelter?
choices: A safe place to stay warm and dry
check.why: A nest or a hole is shelter. It keeps an animal safe, warm and dry.

check.q: How is an animal different from a plant?
choices: An animal does not need water
An animal must find its food
An animal does not need air
check.why: Plants make their own food. Animals must eat plants or other animals.

check.q: A fish gets air from...
check.why: Gills pull air out of the water. That is how a fish breathes.

lessons.title: Who Eats What
lessons.mainIdea: Some animals eat plants. Some animals eat other animals. Some eat both.
reading: All animals need food. Food gives them *energy* to move and grow. But animals eat different things. A cow eats grass. A hawk eats mice. A raccoon eats berries and frogs.
A rabbit eats plants. A fox eats the rabbit. The fox got its energy from the rabbit. The rabbit got it from plants. The plants got it from the sun. This is a *food chain*.
Look at teeth for clues. Flat teeth grind plants. Sharp, pointy teeth tear meat. Your teeth have both kinds. People can eat plants and meat.

words.d: what living things use to move, grow and stay warm; it comes from food
a line that shows who eats what

look.title: A Meal on the Prairie
look.text: A grasshopper chews a blade of grass. A frog snaps up the grasshopper. A snake swallows the frog. A hawk swoops down and grabs the snake.
look.prompt: Where did the hawk's energy come from at the very start of the chain?

check.q: A cow has flat teeth. What does it eat?
check.why: Flat teeth grind plants. Cows chew grass all day.

check.q: Where does a fox get its energy?
check.why: A fox cannot make food from sunlight. It gets energy by eating rabbits and mice.

check.q: Which one is a food chain?
check.why: A food chain shows who eats what. The rabbit eats grass, and the fox eats the rabbit.

lessons.title: Plants and Animals Change Places
lessons.mainIdea: Living things change the places where they live.
reading: Have you seen a bumpy sidewalk? Tree roots did that. Roots grow thick and strong. They push the concrete up. Slowly, the sidewalk cracks.
A squirrel buries *acorns* in the fall. It forgets some of them. In spring, a tiny oak pops up. The squirrel planted a tree without knowing it.
A beaver cuts down small trees with its teeth. It builds a *dam* across a stream. Water backs up. A pond forms. Frogs and ducks move in. One animal changed the whole place.

words.d: the seed of an oak tree
a wall across a stream that holds back water

look.title: The Bumpy Sidewalk
look.text: A big tree grows next to a sidewalk. Each year the trunk gets wider. Its roots grow long under the ground. The sidewalk slabs tilt up. Now there is a bump you could trip on.
look.prompt: What pushed the sidewalk up? What might happen in ten more years?

check.q: What cracks a sidewalk next to a tree?
check.why: Roots grow thick and strong. They push the concrete up until it cracks.

check.q: A squirrel forgets a buried acorn. What may happen?
choices: The acorn turns into a rock
check.why: An acorn is a seed. Left in the dirt, it can sprout into an oak.

check.q: What does a beaver dam make?
check.why: The dam holds back the stream. Water backs up and makes a pond.

lessons.title: People Change the Land Too
lessons.mainIdea: People change the land, and people can take care of it.
reading: People change the land a lot. We build roads. We build houses. We cut trees. We plant corn and beans in big fields. The land under Chicago was once *prairie* and marsh. Now it is a big city.
Changes can hurt living things. When a field becomes a parking lot, mice and birds lose their homes. Trash in a creek can hurt fish.
People can help too. We can plant trees. We can pick up trash. We can leave a corner of the yard wild for bees. In Illinois, people plant new prairies. Butterflies come back.

words.d: land covered with tall grass and wildflowers, with few trees

look.title: Two Schoolyards
look.text: Schoolyard A is all blacktop. Schoolyard B has a garden, a few trees and a patch of tall grass. On a spring day, you count the birds and bees at each one.
look.prompt: Which schoolyard has more living things? Why do you think so?

check.q: What was the land under Chicago long ago?
check.why: Before the city, the land was tall grass and wet marsh. People changed it.

check.q: A field becomes a parking lot. What happens to the mice?
check.why: The field was their shelter and food. Blacktop takes that away.

check.q: Which is a way to take care of the land?
choices: Plant trees and pick up trash
check.why: Trees and clean creeks give living things food, water and shelter.

review.why: A rock does not grow, eat or make more rocks. Worms and dandelions do grow.

review.q: What three things does a plant need to grow?
review.why: Roots drink water. Leaves catch light and take in air.

review.q: Mia forgot to water her bean. The leaves drooped. Why?
review.why: Without water, the leaves went limp. After a drink, they stood up again.

review.q: Which need does a bird's nest meet?
review.why: A nest is a safe place. It keeps the bird and its eggs warm and hidden.

review.q: A hawk eats a snake. The snake ate a frog. The frog ate a grasshopper. Where did the grasshopper's energy come from?
review.why: The chain starts with plants. The grasshopper ate grass, and grass got energy from the sun.

review.q: How can a tree change a sidewalk?
choices: Its roots push it up and crack it
review.why: Roots grow thick under the concrete and slowly lift it.

chapters.title: Parents, Young and Habitats
chapters.bigQuestion: How do living things fit the places where they live?

story.title: Who Lives on the Prairie?
story.kicker: Grass taller than you. Buzzing, hopping, singing. Who is out here?
paragraphs: In June, Ms. Ortiz took her class to a prairie near Chicago. The grass was tall. Some of it was taller than the kids. Purple and yellow flowers poked up. The wind made the grass wave like water.
Jamal stood very still. A grasshopper jumped past his shoe. A bee landed on a purple flower. It walked around. Then it flew to another flower. Yellow dust stuck to its legs.
Then they heard a song. A small bird sat on a tall stem. It sang and sang. Ms. Ortiz said it was a meadowlark. Its nest was hidden down in the grass. Baby birds were waiting for food.

Near the path, a rabbit froze. Two smaller rabbits froze too. They looked just like their mother. Only smaller. Ms. Ortiz said, "This is their home. It gives them everything they need." The class walked on, quietly.
story.think: The bee, the meadowlark and the rabbits all live in the prairie. What does the prairie give each one?

lessons.title: Young Look Like Their Parents
lessons.mainIdea: Young plants and animals look like their parents, but not exactly.
reading: A kitten looks like a cat. It has fur, four legs and whiskers. But it is smaller. Its fur may be a different color. It is like its *parent*, but not the same.
A baby rabbit looks like its mother. A puppy looks like a dog. A baby oak tree has oak leaves. *Young* things grow up to look more like their parents.
Some young look very different at first. A tadpole has a tail and no legs. Then it grows legs. Its tail shrinks. It becomes a frog, like its parents.

words.d: a mother or a father
a baby animal or a new, small plant

look.title: A Litter of Puppies
look.text: A brown dog has five puppies. Three are brown. One is black. One is white with brown spots. All five have floppy ears and a long tail, just like their mother.
look.prompt: How are the puppies like their mother? How are they different?

check.q: A kitten is like its mother. But it may have...
check.why: Young look like their parents, but not exactly. Color and size can be different.

check.q: What grows from an acorn?
choices: An oak tree, like the parent tree
check.why: An acorn is an oak seed. The young tree grows oak leaves like its parent.

check.q: A tadpole grows up to be...
check.why: A tadpole grows legs and loses its tail. It becomes a frog like its parents.

lessons.title: Parents Take Care of Young
lessons.mainIdea: Many animal parents feed, warm and protect their young.
reading: Baby birds cannot fly. They cannot find food. They open their beaks wide and chirp. The parents fly back and forth all day. They bring worms and bugs.
A mother cat keeps her kittens warm. She licks them clean. A mother deer hides her fawn in tall grass. She comes back to feed it milk. She works to *protect* it.
Not all animals do this. A sea turtle lays her eggs on a beach and leaves. The babies *hatch* alone. They crawl to the sea by themselves.

words.d: to keep safe from harm
to break out of an egg

look.title: Eggs in One Nest
look.prompt: The sea turtle lays the most eggs. She does not stay to care for them. Why might she lay so many?

check.q: Why do baby birds chirp with open beaks?
choices: They want food from their parents
check.why: Baby birds cannot find food. Chirping tells the parents to bring worms.

check.q: A mother deer hides her fawn in tall grass. This keeps the fawn...
check.why: Hiding protects the fawn. The mother comes back to feed it.

check.q: Which animal parent leaves its eggs?
check.why: A sea turtle lays eggs on the beach and goes back to the sea. The babies hatch alone.

lessons.title: Beaks and Claws
lessons.mainIdea: Animals have body parts that help them get food and stay safe.
reading: Look at a bird's *beak*. A duck's beak is wide and flat. It scoops food from water. A hawk's beak is sharp and hooked. It tears meat. A finch's beak is short and thick. It cracks seeds.
*Claws* help too. A cat's claws grip and climb. A squirrel's claws hold onto bark. An eagle's claws grab fish. A mole's wide claws dig through dirt.
Each body part fits a job. You can guess what an animal eats by looking at its beak or claws. Scientists do this all the time.

words.d: the hard mouth of a bird
a sharp, curved nail on an animal's foot

look.title: How Many Legs?
look.prompt: Which animal has the most legs? How do legs help each animal move or hold on?

check.q: A hawk's beak is sharp and hooked. What does it eat?
check.why: A hooked beak tears meat. Hawks eat mice and other small animals.

check.q: What do a mole's wide claws do?
check.why: Moles live under the ground. Wide claws work like little shovels.

check.q: A bird has a short, thick beak. What does it likely eat?
check.why: A short, thick beak cracks hard seeds, like a finch's beak.

lessons.title: Thorns, Fur and Shells
lessons.mainIdea: Plants and animals have parts that protect them.
reading: A rose has *thorns*. A deer wants to eat the leaves. Ouch! The thorns poke its nose. The deer walks away. Thorns protect the plant.
A rabbit has thick fur. Fur keeps it warm in an Illinois winter. A turtle has a hard shell. It pulls its head inside. A fox cannot bite through.
A skunk has a stinky spray. A porcupine has sharp quills. A cactus has spines and a thick skin that holds water. Each part helps the living thing *survive*.

words.d: a sharp point on a plant stem
to stay alive

look.title: A Turtle by the Pond
look.text: A raccoon finds a turtle by the pond. The turtle pulls its head and legs into its shell. The raccoon pokes and paws at it. The shell stays shut. The raccoon gives up and leaves.
look.prompt: What did the shell do for the turtle? Name another animal with a part that protects it.

check.q: Why does a rose have thorns?
choices: To keep animals from eating it
check.why: Thorns poke any animal that tries to eat the leaves. The plant stays safe.

check.q: What does thick fur do for a rabbit?
check.why: Fur holds in heat. It helps the rabbit survive cold winters.

check.q: A cactus has a thick skin. It helps the cactus...
check.why: The desert is dry. Thick skin keeps the cactus from losing its water.

lessons.title: Pond and Forest
lessons.mainIdea: Different kinds of living things live in different places.
reading: A *habitat* is the place where a living thing lives. It gives food, water, air and shelter. A pond is a habitat. A forest is a habitat.
In a pond, frogs sit on lily pads. Ducks dip for plants. Dragonflies zip over the water. Fish hide in the weeds. Cattails grow at the edge.
In a forest, tall trees make shade. Owls sleep in holes in the trunks. Deer eat leaves. Squirrels leap from branch to branch. Mushrooms grow on old logs.

words.d: the place where a plant or animal lives and gets what it needs

look.title: The Wrong Home
look.text: Imagine a duck in a forest with no water. Imagine an owl in a pond with no trees. Now switch them. Put the duck on the pond and the owl in the forest.
look.prompt: Why does each animal fit its own habitat? What does each one need?

check.q: What is a habitat?
choices: The place where a living thing lives
check.why: A habitat gives a living thing its food, water, air and shelter.

check.q: Which animal fits a pond habitat?
check.why: Frogs need water. A pond gives them water, bugs to eat and lily pads to sit on.

check.q: Why do owls live in forests?
choices: There is lots of open water
Trees give them holes to sleep in
check.why: An owl needs shelter. A hole in a tree trunk is a safe place to rest.

lessons.title: Prairie and Desert
lessons.mainIdea: A prairie and a desert are very different habitats with their own living things.
reading: Illinois is called the Prairie State. A *prairie* is a sea of tall grass and flowers. Few trees grow there. Grasshoppers, meadowlarks and rabbits live on the prairie.
Prairie grass has very deep roots. Some roots go down deeper than a grown-up is tall. Deep roots find water. They help the grass live through dry summers and cold winters.
A *desert* is dry. Little rain falls. Days are hot. A cactus stores water in its stem. A lizard hides under a rock in the heat. A kangaroo rat gets water from the seeds it eats.

words.d: land of tall grass and wildflowers, with few trees
a very dry place that gets little rain

look.title: Rain in One Year
look.prompt: Which place is a desert? How can you tell from the numbers?

check.q: Why does prairie grass have deep roots?
check.why: Deep roots reach water far below. That helps the grass live through dry summers.

check.q: A desert is...
check.why: Deserts get little rain. Plants and animals there must save water.

check.q: How does a cactus live in a dry desert?
choices: It stores water in its stem
check.why: A cactus keeps water inside its thick stem for the long dry times.

lessons.title: Pollen and Traveling Seeds
lessons.mainIdea: Animals help plants make seeds and carry seeds to new places.
reading: Remember the bee on the purple flower? Yellow dust stuck to its legs. That dust is *pollen*. The bee carried it to the next flower. Now that flower can make seeds.
Bees, butterflies and hummingbirds do this. They are *pollinators*. The flower gives them sweet nectar. They give the flower a ride for its pollen. Both win.
Seeds travel too. A dandelion seed floats on the wind. A burr sticks to a dog's fur. A bird eats a berry and drops the seed far away. New plants grow in new places.

words.d: yellow dust from a flower that helps it make seeds
an animal that carries pollen from flower to flower

look.title: Socks After a Hike
look.text: You walk through tall grass in the fall. Back home, your socks are covered in little sticky seeds. You pull them off and drop them in the yard.
look.prompt: How did the seeds travel? What might grow in your yard next spring?

check.q: What is pollen?
choices: Yellow dust that helps a flower make seeds
check.why: Pollen is the yellow dust on a flower. When it moves to another flower, seeds can form.

check.q: What does a flower give a bee?
check.why: The bee drinks nectar. In return, it carries the flower's pollen.

check.q: How does a dandelion seed travel?
check.why: Dandelion seeds have fluffy tops. The wind carries them to new places.

review.q: How is a puppy like its parents?
choices: It has fur and four legs like them
It is exactly the same size
review.why: Young look like their parents, but they are smaller and may be a different color.

review.q: Which parent feeds its babies worms?
review.why: Robin parents bring worms and bugs to the nest all day.

review.q: A duck's wide, flat beak is good for...
review.why: A wide, flat beak scoops up plants and bugs from the pond.

review.q: What does a turtle's shell do?
review.why: The turtle pulls inside its hard shell. Other animals cannot bite through.

review.q: Which habitat has tall grass and few trees?
review.why: A prairie is a sea of grass and flowers. Illinois is the Prairie State.

review.q: A burr sticks to a dog's fur. What is the burr doing?
choices: Traveling to a new place to grow
review.why: A burr is a seed. Sticking to fur is how it gets to new places.
